deep.reconstruction:
The page is not a derivation. It continues a table of the full repeating periods of the decimal expansions of 1/p, running downward through the primes. This leaf covers p = 701, 683, 677, 673, 661, 659. The previous leaf has 739 down to 691 and the next has 653 down to 613. Primes the table does not list may have been skipped or are on other leaves.

Notation: Gauss writes each period starting at its first non-zero digit. Every 1/p here begins 0.00…, so the two leading zeros appear at the end of his row. Each period is therefore written as a cyclic rotation. He then writes the first few digits of the period again, underlined, followed by '…', to show it repeats.

The period length is ord_p(10). Counting digits on the page gives (counting is mine):
- 701: 10 lines of 7 ten-digit groups = 700 digits, ending '…4251069900'. Period 700, so 10 is a primitive root mod 701.
- 683: 4×70 + 60 + 1 = 341 digits ('…4392386530' then '0'), then '1464128 84' repeats. ord = 341 = 682/2.
- 677: 280 + 50 + 8 = 338 digits ('39438700'), then '14' repeats. ord = 338 = 676/2.
- 673: 210 + 10 + 4 = 224 digits ('6300'), then '148588' repeats. ord = 224 = 672/3.
- 661: 210 + 10 = 220 digits, then '1512859304' repeats. ord = 220 = 660/3.
- 659: 630 + 28 = 658 digits ('…89226100'), then '15' repeats. ord = 658, so 10 is a primitive root mod 659.

The periods were presumably produced by long division (or by multiplying known blocks). The values of ord_p(10) agree with quadratic-residue considerations (my check):
- For 683 and 677, (10/p) = (2/p)(5/p) = (−1)(−1) = +1, so the order divides (p−1)/2.
- For 673, 661 and 659, 10 is a non-residue, so the order keeps the full 2-part of p−1 (32 | 224, 4 | 220).

When the period length 2m is even, 10^m ≡ −1 (mod p), so digit i and digit i+m of the period sum to 9 (Midy's property). I used this to spot-check the table. Every check below succeeds:
- 701, m = 350: line 1 against line 6 and line 2 against line 7 are digit-wise complementary.
- 659, m = 329: digits 1–11 against 330–340; groups at digits 121–130 against 450–459; digits 421–430 against 92–101.
- 677, m = 169: digit 1 ↔ 170, digits 2–11 ↔ 171–180, and digit 160 ↔ 329.
- 673, m = 112: digit 1 ↔ 113.
- 661, m = 110: digits 1–3 ↔ 111–113.

Purpose: this is part of Gauss's table for converting common fractions with prime denominators into decimal fractions. It relates to Disquisitiones Arithmeticae arts. 312–318, where he explains how such a table, combined with indices (discrete logarithms) to base 10, gives the decimal expansion of any fraction a/p by cyclic shifting.
errors: No arithmetic errors detected in the spot checks (complementary-digit tests for 701, 659, 677, 673, 661, and the leading digits of every entry).

Two digits are visibly overwritten or corrected in the manuscript: the final digit of '4505169867' in the 677 entry and the final digit of '6039453717' in the 659 entry. The complement test confirms the corrected values (7 and 7) are right.
The red pencil strokes across the 677/673 block are probably a checking or cancellation mark, not a correction of digits.

results.what: Full decimal periods of 1/p for p = 701, 683, 677, 673, 661, 659, with period lengths 700, 341, 338, 224, 220, 658 (= ord_p 10)
results.modern_name: Table of repetends (decimal periods) of reciprocals of primes; multiplicative order of 10 mod p
results.usually_credited_to: Decimal-period tables: J. H. Lambert, J. Bernoulli III, H. Goodwyn (1818-1823), Burckhardt; Gauss's own table was published posthumously in Werke II (1863)

results.what: Consistency of period lengths with the quadratic character of 10 (ord divides (p-1)/2 iff 10 is a QR) and the half-period nines-complement property
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (criterion); E. Midy 1836 (complement property), known earlier to Gauss (DA art. 312ff)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a page of Gauss's well-known computational table of decimal periods of 1/p, the kind of table described in Disquisitiones arts. 312-318 and printed in Werke II. It is pure routine computation with no new method or result.
